So Requity was born — a program that sends vocational students across the street from their Baltimore high school to rehab abandoned homes, turning classroom skills into real jobs and real neighborhoods. stories.title: "When we watched Durham do that, we decided that was a fight we needed to have in Asheville."
stories.summary: After a 10-month campaign, Asheville's city council voted unanimously to make it illegal for landlords to collect rent on properties the city has deemed unsafe. Organizers with the Asheville Area Tenants Union say they were inspired by Durham's similar ordinance — and now Asheville joins a growing list of NC cities protecting renters.
stories.extended_summary: Ten months of organizing ended with a unanimous vote: in Asheville, landlords can no longer collect rent on properties the city has flagged as unsafe. The ordinance kicks in when a landlord ignores a violation notice for any of 18 criteria — no hot water, no heat, no smoke detector. Organizer Rachel Wyse, a lifelong Asheville resident, said the campaign was inspired by watching Durham pass its own version. "When we watched Durham do that, we decided that was a fight we needed to have in Asheville." The city now joins Durham, Charlotte, Pineville, and Pittsboro in a growing North Carolina movement to stop landlords from profiting off uninhabitable housing.

stories.title: Carving Out a Niche
stories.summary: Joe Schneider spent years building cabinets before turning his engineering background and love of woodworking into Wood Slab King, a business that turns salvaged urban trees into one-of-a-kind live-edge slabs. He and his nephew Andrew Craney rescue logs from tree services and give fallen trees a second life as furniture and art.
stories.extended_summary: Every slab that leaves Wood Slab King started as a tree that was coming down anyway — damaged, dangerous, or in the way. Joe Schneider and his nephew Andrew Craney salvage those logs through a process called urban salvage, cutting them on a sawmill that handles slabs up to 53 inches wide and 17 feet long. The wood is full of surprises: they've pulled clothesline hooks, dog chains, butter knives, and even a crucifix out of the timber. Then comes the patience — two to three years of air drying before a single piece is ready. No two slabs are alike, and that's the whole point.
